 USDA Has Opened an Active E. coli O157:H7 Investigation With Ground Beef as the Suspect. No Recall, No Alert, No Case Count. The Same Morning CDC Added Three E. coli Files to Its Dashboard, None With a Notice.
 By Bill Marler on November 18, 2026 
 Posted in Food Poisoning Information 
 As of November 18, 2026, the Food Safety and Inspection Service’s  outbreak investigations table  carries a new row: investigation 2027-01, dated October 2026, pathogen  E. coli  O157:H7, product “Ground Beef (suspect),” Active: Yes. The row has no case count, no states, no hospitalization or HUS number, no recall and no public health alert attached to it. The same morning, CDC’s  current outbreaks dashboard  moved from 26 to 27 active multistate investigations, with the  E. coli  line going from three to six. No notice accompanied any of them.
 The row is the first of USDA’s fiscal 2027 and the first ground beef O157 file since 2024 
 FSIS numbers its investigations by federal fiscal year, which begins October 1. The last ground beef  E. coli O157:H7 row on the table was 2025-03, the November 2024 outbreak that ended with Wolverine Packing Co. recalling  about 167,277 pounds  after Minnesota tied fifteen illnesses to ground beef. Before that, the table shows a run of “Beef, ground (suspect)” rows from 2021 through 2023, most of them closed with no outcome listed at all.
 When I  wrote about the tables on October 23 , FSIS listed one active investigation for all of 2026, the chicken wrap file it shares with FDA as 2026-04. The ground beef row was posted sometime after that. FSIS says it updates the table at least weekly and posts an investigation only when there is compelling epidemiologic, sampling or traceback evidence that a meat, poultry or egg product is a confirmed or suspected source. By the agency’s own rule, that evidence exists for this file.
 What the table says, and what it does not 
 Here is everything the public can learn from FSIS about this outbreak today.
 Field What FSIS has published 
 Investigation number 2027-01 
 Outbreak month October 2026 
 Pathogen E. coli  O157:H7 
 Product Ground beef (suspect) 
 Active Yes 
 Case count Not published 
 States Not published 
 Hospitalizations and HUS Not published 
 Recall or public health alert None 
 CDC notice None 
 Establishment or retailer Not published 
 FSIS outbreak investigations table, read November 18, 2026. Check: of twelve fields a sick person would want, five are filled and seven are blank. 
 Compare the row to its neighbor. The chicken wrap file, 2026-04, was posted with no product either, and it took a courthouse filing, then  an email from FSIS to a reporter , before anyone outside the agencies learned which wrap it was. I made the case then that  fifty sick people and a known supplier  deserve a name. The ground beef file starts the same way: a product category and a word, suspect.
 Ground beef is the one food where FSIS already has the tools to say more 
 FSIS declared  E. coli  O157:H7 an adulterant in raw ground beef in 1994, after Jack in the Box. Since then the agency has sampled ground beef for O157 at federally inspected plants, at import, and at retail, and it has treated a positive lot in commerce as a Class I recall. That program is why I am no longer in the hamburger business. The firm’s  E. coli  cases ran from Jack in the Box in 1993 to the ConAgra recall in 2002, and ground beef is now a small fraction of our docket. I have called the adulterant rule the best thing to happen in food safety in my lifetime, and I meant it.
 That history is also why an active ground beef O157 file with no public action is worth stopping on. In the Kebab Shop outbreak this spring, FSIS collected product, found O157:H7 in the kofta, matched it to patients by whole genome sequencing, and  issued a public health alert naming the restaurants and the producer  even though the product was long gone. That is the agency’s normal practice when it has a match. An October outbreak that is still active in the third week of November, with ground beef as the suspect and no alert, means one of two things: the traceback has not reached a lot, or it has and nobody has been assigned to tell the public.
 CDC’s dashboard moved the same morning, and the three new  E. coli  files have no notices either 
 CDC’s dashboard counts the multistate investigations it is coordinating each week. On November 12 it read 26: 15  Salmonella , 3  E. coli , 4  Listeria , 4  Campylobacter . On November 18 it reads 27: 15  Salmonella , 6  E. coli , 4  Listeria , 2  Campylobacter . Three  E. coli  investigations were added in six days. Whether one of them is FSIS 2027-01, or the Ohio University cluster, or something nobody has heard of yet, the dashboard does not say. CDC posts an outbreak notice only when it has advice for the public, and no  E. coli  notice has been posted since the Graziers raw milk cheese closure on November 13.
 Date Active Salmonella E. coli Listeria Campylobacter 
 November 5 28 16 7 3 2 
 November 12 26 15 3 4 4 
 November 18 27 15 6 4 2 
 CDC current outbreaks dashboard, as posted on each date. Check: 15 + 6 + 4 + 2 = 27. 
 What FSIS should publish this week 
 The row already tells industry and the trade press that FSIS has a ground beef O157 file open. It should tell the rest of us the same things it told the public in May: how many people are sick, in which states, how many are hospitalized, how many children have HUS, when the illnesses began, and whether a product sample has matched a patient by sequencing. If a lot has been identified, name the establishment and issue the alert even if the product is past its use-by date; that is exactly what the agency did for the kofta. If the traceback has not reached a lot, say that, so the word suspect carries its honest meaning.
 I have been asking all fall for the agencies to say what they know while people are still getting sick. The ground beef program is the proof that FSIS can do it. A plant that ships a positive lot gets a Class I recall within days. An outbreak that has been open since October should get at least a sentence.
